parsed.main_gap: Negative values of g are never excluded: §3 only rules out two distinct positive values, yet the dichotomy 'g≡0 or V⊆{0,c}' silently assumes g≥0 everywhere.

errors.description: The classification jumps from 'V contains at most one positive number' to 'V ⊆ {0} or V ⊆ {0,c}', without ruling out g(x)<0 for some x. This case is never treated, so the case analysis (and Lemma 1, which assumes b∈{0,c}) is incomplete. (Repairable in two lines: if g(x₀)=-d<0, iterating (4) gives g(x₀-nd)=-d and x₀-nd>0 for all n, impossible.)
errors.quote:
Thus $V$ contains **at most one** positive number.  Consequently, either  

* (i) $g\equiv 0$ (constant), which gives $f(x)=x$, a solution; or  
* (ii) there is $c>0$ such that $V \subseteq \{0, c\}$ with both values attainable.

errors.description: Sign/variable typo in the specialization of A: with a=0, b=c the formula gives (x−y)²+4cy+2c², not 4cx. Harmless (conclusion 'always true' is unaffected), but it is an error in the displayed identity.

In the irrational-ratio case the existence of approximating pairs with n_k,m_k→∞ is asserted rather than argued; density gives values close to the target but the divergence of indices needs a one-line remark (or the observation that exact equality already yields a contradiction). Minor.
errors.quote: Hence we can choose sequences $(n_k,m_k)\to(\infty,\infty)$ with $n_k c_1 - m_k c_2 \to -(u - v - c_2)$.

parsed.notes: Answer correct and verified; derivation of f(f(y))=2f(y)−y, identities (5)–(7), the two-positive-values argument, Lemma 1 and the covering argument are all correct and well executed. One omitted case (g<0) prevents full marks.
